A BRIEF HISTORY OF STUDENT GROWTH
 PROMISES FULFILLED & OPPORTUNITIES MISSED

 Damian W Betebenner
 National Center for the Improvement of Educational Assessment
 CCSSO/NCSA Orlando, FL June 25th, 2019
 dbetebenner@nciea.org @dbetebenner

My Background
• Began investigating large scale longitudinal analyses in 1999 as a
 graduate student at the University of Colorado, Boulder.

• Investigated/replicated EVAAS and other VAMs, Markov-chain/
 transition matrices, growth curve/HLM models in early 2000s.

• Developed Student Growth Percentile (SGP) methodology in
 2005-2007 while a professor at Boston College.

• Joined the Center for Assessment in 2007 and over the last 12 years
 have worked with over 40 states and several consortia and testing
 companies on the calculation and use of student growth.

Promises Fulfilled
• All states have investigated and nearly every state has adopted/
 utilized an individual student growth model.
• States and testing vendors are very interested in calculating student
 growth in almost all contexts in which they have longitudinal student
 achievement data.
• There is MUCH greater understanding of student growth amongst
 state level personnel (far exceeding what academics know). State
 level personnel, in general, know what they are talking about.
• States recognize that a vertical scale doesn’t solve all the growth
 issues and are taking advantage of both norm- and criterion-
 referenced growth.
• States recognize and are taking advantage of both norm- and
 criterion-referenced growth.

Opportunities Missed (thus far)
• Broadly, we are much better at using data as a hammer than as a
 flashlight.
• Student growth has primarily been used as part of state accountability
 initiatives. For example, school and teacher evaluations.
• Student growth has, in general, not been used to investigate:

 • Issues related to equity: For example, growth gaps between demographic
 subgroups.
 • Issues related to assessment bias: For example, test mode of administration
 effects.
 • Issues related to program evaluation: For example, investigating whether
 programs or curricula are associated with exemplary student growth.
 • Issues related to diagnosis of individual strengths/weaknesses.

• Policy makers don’t understand the implications of what growth-to-
 standard analyses imply.

Growth Gaps
• The analysis of student growth can enable powerful discussions about
 equal educational opportunity.
• Even after accounting for where students start, students from
 disadvantaged subgroups demonstrate less academic growth than
 students from advantaged subgroups.
 • Median/mean SGPs for disadvantaged subgroups are almost always in
 the mid to low 40s where as advantaged groups are usually in mid 50s.
• Using growth analyses to identify districts and schools with extreme
 growth gaps or reverse growth gaps supports powerful discussions
 about equity.
• Conversely, including demographic adjustments in growth analyses
 themselves adjusts out these differences and sweeps the problem under
 the rug.

Assessment Bias

• Regression based growth analyses (e.g. SGP) which utilize students’ prior
 scores act like a propensity score based analysis.
• SGP analyses in the past have detected mode effects between paper and
 pencil and computer administered tests that appeared inconsequential
 when looked at using only current attainment.
• SGP analyses have also detected substantial differences in the growth of
 subgroups when states have transitioned to different tests.
• Beyond accountability, disparate growth results can quickly and easily
 highlight issues related to to the testing system itself — but it is rarely
 used in this fashion.

Program Evaluation

• Again, regression based growth analyses (e.g. SGP) which utilize students’
 prior scores act like a propensity score analysis.
• States, districts, schools often have local knowledge about student group
 membership that can be used to quickly and easily investigate impact.
 • A school district in MA noticed unusually low student growth amongst
 4th graders. This district had K-3 schools followed by a transition to
 4-6. The transition was likely impacting student growth.
 • With growth results over multiple years, the impact of curricular
 changes can be investigated to see whether they lead to increased
 student growth.

 associated with extraordinary levels of attainment.
